data.content_ref: inline:SRC_002's 'Plausible Decoy' mechanism lacks a causal link to reliability: a decoy that is 'logically consistent with the process but irrelevant to the correct outcome' tests whether a panel will reject an instruction, but rejecting instructions is neither necessary nor sufficient for objectively verifiable reliability. A panel that blindly trusts expert-built checklists can be highly reliable yet 'fail' the decoy, while a non-expert panel that rejects the decoy for the wrong idiosyncratic reason can score high on the probe while failing real items. SRC_002 asserts that rejecting a plausible decoy is 'the hallmark of reliability over obedience,' but it provides no causal mechanism mapping decoy rejection to lower error rate on the target task. Its own counterconditions concede both experts being fooled and instructions forbidding questioning, undermining any task-reliability inference.
